title: Diversity and respectful talk
goal: Plan around six religions and their holidays, wish people well at the right feast in the right words, and handle a personal question about faith gracefully — from either side of the table.
bekal: talk about religious holidays and dates: *jatuh pada*, *bentrok dengan*, *cuti bersama*
give the right greeting for Idul Fitri, Natal, Nyepi, Waisak and Imlek
answer (and ask) a sensitive question with tact: *doakan saja*, *urusan pribadi*, *saling menghormati*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Kalender kegiatan 2030
dialogs.intro: October 2029. The first group of Australian students for next year has been confirmed, and Sarah and Fajar sit down with a blank calendar and two cups of coffee.

notes: **Jatuh pada** — a holiday "falls on" a date, exactly as in English: *Natal jatuh pada hari Rabu*. Fajar's *jatuhnya* is the spoken, *-nya* version. Islamic holidays follow the lunar calendar and move about eleven days earlier every year, which is why Lebaran, which fell in mid-February in 2029, lands in early February in 2030.

**Cuti bersama** — "collective leave": extra days the government adds around big holidays, especially Lebaran, so the whole country can travel home. Offices close and the roads fill. Never schedule anything important in that week.

**Nyepi** is the Balinese Hindu new year (*Tahun Baru Saka*), a day of complete silence: no lights, no traffic, no flights, and even tourists stay in their hotels. The night before, the loud *ogoh-ogoh* parades drive evil spirits away; the silence then persuades them nobody is home.

**Itu ibadah, bukan tontonan** — "it is worship, not a spectacle". Waisak at Borobudur draws thousands of photographers every year, and Buddhist communities have repeatedly asked visitors to keep their distance. *X, bukan Y* is the cleanest way in Indonesian to correct a frame.

**Salat Jumat** — Friday midday prayers, obligatory for Muslim men. Offices and schools effectively pause from around 11.30 to 13.00, so meetings are never set for that slot. The standard spelling is *salat*; *sholat* and *shalat* are common but not baku.

**Ini baru namanya…** — "now THAT is what you call…". *Baru* here is not "new" but "only now, at last": *Ini baru enak!* (now this is tasty). 💬 Fajar's *dimatiin* is Jakarta for *dimatikan*, and *gila-gilaan* ("crazily") means "like mad".

grammars.title: Greetings for every faith
body: Indonesia officially recognises six religions, and everyone learns the greetings for each other's feasts. Getting the pairing right is a small act of respect that people notice.

head: Feast
Faith
Greeting
rows: *Selamat Idul Fitri, mohon maaf lahir dan batin.*
*Selamat Hari Raya Nyepi, Tahun Baru Saka.*
*Selamat Tahun Baru Imlek. Gong Xi Fa Cai!*

after: *Hari raya* is a religious feast; *hari libur nasional* is any public holiday, which also includes *17 Agustus* and *Tahun Baru*. The formal umbrella term is *hari besar keagamaan*.

⚠️ Whether Muslims should wish Christians *Selamat Natal* is argued over every December. Most say it freely; some do not. If a colleague answers your *Selamat Natal* with a simple *terima kasih* and no greeting back, take no offence.

grammars.title: Dates that meet and clash
body: Planning a calendar in Indonesian needs a handful of verbs for how dates relate to each other.
after: *Bertepatan dengan* is neutral or even happy (*bertepatan dengan ulang tahunnya*); *bentrok* always means a problem. In formal writing, *berbenturan dengan* is a slightly more elegant alternative to *bentrok*.

dialogs.title: Second dialogue — Pertanyaan yang pribadi
dialogs.intro: A week later, Sarah gives a talk about the programme at a partner senior high school in East Jakarta. In the question session, a Year 11 student called Nadia puts her hand up.

lines.speaker: Nadia:
lines.text: Miss Sarah, boleh tanya yang agak pribadi?
lines.id: Miss Sarah, may I ask something a bit personal?
lines.literal: Miss Sarah, may ask which rather private?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Boleh, asal saya juga boleh tidak menjawab, ya.
lines.id: You may, as long as I'm allowed not to answer.
lines.literal: may, provided I also may not answer, [ya].

lines.speaker: Nadia:
lines.text: Agama Miss apa? Di Australia orang masih ke gereja?
lines.id: What's your religion, Miss? Do people in Australia still go to church?
lines.literal: religion Miss what? in Australia people still to church?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Pertanyaan yang bagus. Di Australia, agama biasanya dianggap urusan pribadi, jadi jarang ditanyakan kepada orang yang baru dikenal.
lines.id: Good question. In Australia religion is usually considered a private matter, so people rarely ask someone they've just met.
lines.literal: question which good. in Australia, religion usually be-considered matter private, so rarely be-asked to person who just-now be-known.

lines.speaker: Nadia:
lines.text: Oh, maaf, Miss. Di sini kan biasa. Di KTP juga ada.
lines.id: Oh, sorry, Miss. Here it's normal, you know. It's even on our ID cards.
lines.literal: oh, sorry, Miss. at here [kan] usual. at KTP also exist.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Nggak apa-apa, saya paham. Saya dibesarkan dalam keluarga Katolik. Di Indonesia saya belajar bahwa orang bisa berbeda keyakinan, tetapi tetap saling menjaga.
lines.id: That's all right, I understand. I was brought up in a Catholic family. In Indonesia I've learnt that people can hold different beliefs and still look out for each other.
lines.literal: not what-what, I understand. I be-raised in family Catholic. in Indonesia I learn that people can differ belief, but still mutual guard.

lines.speaker: Nadia:
lines.text: Kayak di kampung saya, Miss. Kalau Lebaran, tetangga yang Kristen ikut bantu masak ketupat.
lines.id: Like in my neighbourhood, Miss. At Lebaran the Christian neighbours help make the ketupat.
lines.literal: like in village my, Miss. if Lebaran, neighbour who Christian join help cook ketupat.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Nah, itu yang sering bikin orang Australia kagum. Toleransi di sini tidak hanya dibicarakan, tetapi dikerjakan.
lines.id: Well, that's what often amazes Australians. Tolerance here isn't just talked about, it's done.

lines.speaker: Nadia:

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Sama sekali tidak. Bertanya dengan hormat justru awal dari saling mengenal.
lines.id: Not at all. Asking respectfully is actually where getting to know each other begins.
lines.literal: same at-all not. ask with respect precisely beginning of mutual know.

notes: **Miss** is what Indonesian pupils call a female English-speaking teacher or guest, from the English-medium course tradition; a man is *Mister*. It is affectionate, not odd, and Sarah answers to it happily.
**Boleh, asal…** — "yes, provided…". Sarah grants permission and keeps a door open for herself in the same breath. *Asal* (or *asalkan*) sets a condition: *Boleh pinjam, asal dikembalikan besok.*

**Urusan pribadi** — "a private matter". *Urusan* is a matter or business that belongs to someone: *Itu urusan saya* (that's my business) is blunt, while *dianggap urusan pribadi* describes a norm without accusing anyone.

**Di KTP juga ada.** The Indonesian identity card (*KTP*) has a religion field. Since a 2017 Constitutional Court ruling, followers of indigenous faiths may enter *Kepercayaan terhadap Tuhan Yang Maha Esa* instead of one of the six religions. Asking about faith is therefore routine here, not intrusive.

**Saling menjaga** — "looking out for each other". *Saling* + verb makes any action mutual: *saling menghormati* (respect each other), *saling membantu*. It is the backbone of every speech on *kerukunan* (inter-faith harmony).

**Tidak hanya dibicarakan, tetapi dikerjakan** — a balanced, formal pair: "not only talked about but done". The full pattern is *tidak hanya … tetapi juga …*; Sarah drops *juga* for punch, which is perfectly acceptable. 💬 In speech: *nggak cuma diomongin, tapi dikerjain*.

grammars.title: Personal questions, graceful answers
body: Several questions that feel intrusive to a Westerner are small talk in Indonesia. You need not answer them fully, but answering with a smile is a skill.

head: Question
What it really means
Graceful answer
rows: *Saya Katolik.* / *Saya tidak beragama, tapi saya menghormati semua agama.*

after: *Doakan saja* ("just pray for me") is the national escape hatch: warm, polite, and it ends the topic. It works for marriage, children, job applications and exams.

⚠️ *Tidak beragama* (having no religion) is legal but unusual to say aloud outside big-city circles. Many non-religious foreigners prefer to name the faith they were raised in, as Sarah does, which is true and kind at once.

sections.title: Six religions, their places and feasts

blocks.text: The first principle of Pancasila, the state philosophy, is *Ketuhanan Yang Maha Esa* — belief in one supreme God. Six religions are officially recognised, each with its own house of worship and holidays on the national calendar.

*Umat* (community of believers) is the respectful collective noun in every formal text: *umat beragama* (people of faith), *antarumat beragama* (between faiths). ⚠️ Indonesian distinguishes *Kristen* (Protestant) from *Katolik*; calling a Catholic *Kristen* is usually heard as a mistake.

sections.title: SARA and the language of respect

blocks.text: *SARA* stands for *Suku, Agama, Ras, dan Antargolongan* — ethnicity, religion, race and inter-group relations. *Isu SARA* is any topic along those lines that could inflame conflict, and public institutions, advertisers and comedians steer well clear of it.

items: *Menghormati* is respect shown by behaviour; *menghargai* is appreciation, valuing something. You *menghormati* your elders and *menghargai* their advice.
*Keberagaman* (diversity, being varied) and *keagamaan* (religious matters) look alike; the first comes from *ragam*, the second from *agama*.
